This is an idea I've always wanted for reddit. Each subverse can have it's own custom policy. Example of policies:

  • Enable/Disable Downvoat (Already implemented inefficiently in subreddits that hides downvote button using css)
  • Metafilter style pay to participate ($5 or whatever appropriate), this will cut down on a lot of spam, trolls, and eliminate sockpuppet accounts. And as a bonus another avenue for funding Voat.
  • Stackoverflow style point cost for downvoating
  • Minimum characters for comment
  • Minimum age of membership to a subverse for comment/submission
  • Maximum up/downvoat per day/per user

Moderators can choose which set of policies they want to enable, and customize the amount of point rewarded/penalized for activities. This way they can shape what kind of content they want in their subverse. This will also make addition and experimentation of new policies much easier. And for older subverse that want to keep existing policies, they don't have to be affected by site wide policy changes.

This is no test. Bitcoin is under attack. Someone is intentionally slowing down the network to a halt.

I'm not the most savvy when it comes to bitcoin but I have a question.

How exactly do you ddos bitcoin itself??
Bitcoin only does a low number of transactions per minute. My guess is you could create a huge backlog of transactions. I'm guessing though I don't know any better than you

That was my thought too. I guess I understand bitcoin even less than I thought I did. I thought it was decentralized with no way to do something like this. I thought the transactions were basically just between two people with no middle man, unless one or both of the parties is using a third party bitcoin seller.

There's no individual middle-man. But there is a bitcoin network, which is decentralized. Bitcoin miners (software running on computers) manage the network and individual miners (or pools of miners) get paid whenever they are the first to secure a new block.

Not quite. The transaction has to go into the Blockchain. The Blockchain is a large database that is duplicated over many servers on the Bitcoin network. So every transaction that is ever made currently has to go into that database. The rate that transactions can be added to this database is currently limited to about ten per second I think.
7 tps, but these days with average larger transaction size(multisig for example) that tps limit is more like 3 or 4 tps

oh. you definitely need to know about miners (but not so much about how they work). They are a 'trusted' third party as a group, but because they're decentralized, trust is built in as long as most of them are honest.

By submitting many low-fee transactions to fill-up the blocks (remember, currently limited to 1MB of data each). This makes miners go through a lot more work and essentially creates backlog of transactions that don't have a chance to make it into current block. As long as you provide a regular fee to your transactions you'll be fine.

BTW, someone at r/ estimated that the attack costs just a few $k per day, so it could be easily sustained for a long period of time.

This will either force bitcoin to increase number of transactions processed per batch (overdue), or add a fee to discourage clogging networks by spamming transfers (will happen eventually, but not until BTC is mined out).

Overall: BTC is safe and reliable. If a bit slower atm. Good stress test tho'

It means there is a fee market now, but I'm not sure users (or wallet software) are ready for that concept. I guess it forces them to get ready (better sooner than later). This situation kind of supports Peter Todd's replace-by-fee update, so that users can rebroadcast with a higher fee without being forced to wait. It also supports the blocksize increase argument to a degree because it would increase the cost of such an attack, but less so since it would mean the blockchain getting more bloated each time it happens.

A worldwide decentralized ledger is a fantastic concept, but it doesn't have to contain every single transaction no matter how small. Conceptually we should be thinking of it as the basis of a worldwide monetary system, but not necessarily the payment system itself.
